claim: SPICE (Super-fast, Parallel, In-memory Calculation Engine) is the in-memory engine that Amazon Quick Sight uses, and data you import into a dataset rather than querying directly becomes SPICE data.

values.display: Super-fast, Parallel, In-memory Calculation Engine
import data into a dataset rather than using a direct SQL query

evidence.quote: When you import data into a dataset rather than using a direct SQL query, it becomes *SPICE data* because of how it's stored. *SPICE (Super-fast, Parallel, In-memory Calculation Engine)* is the robust in-memory engine that Amazon Quick Sight uses.

claim: Importing data into SPICE makes analytical queries faster, avoids waiting for direct queries, and lets data be reused without additional cost; with a per-query data source you pay when you first create the dataset and on each refresh.
question: Why import data into SPICE instead of using direct query?

values.display: Your analytical queries process faster
reused multiple times without incurring additional costs

evidence.quote: Your analytical queries process faster.

Data stored in SPICE can be reused multiple times without incurring additional costs. If you use a data source that charges per query, you're charged for querying the data when you first create the dataset and later when you refresh the dataset.

claim: In the Enterprise edition of Amazon Quick you can restrict access to a dataset with row-level security (RLS); dataset owners still see all the data while readers see only data allowed by the permission dataset rules.
question: How do you restrict which rows Quick users can see?

values.display: you can restrict access to a dataset by configuring row-level security (RLS) on it
they can only see the data restricted by the permission dataset rules

evidence.quote: In the Enterprise edition of Amazon Quick, you can restrict access to a dataset by configuring row-level security (RLS) on it. You can do this before or after you have shared the dataset. When you share a dataset with RLS with dataset owners, they can still see all the data. When you share it with readers, however, they can only see the data restricted by the permission dataset rules.

claim: Choose user-based RLS rules to secure data for users or groups registered in Quick, and tag-based rules only for embedded dashboards and users not provisioned in Quick.
question: Which Quick RLS rule type fits anonymous embedded users?

values.display: Choose user-based rules if you want to secure data for users or groups provisioned (registered) in Quick
Choose tag-based rules only if you are using embedded dashboards

evidence.quote: Choose user-based rules if you want to secure data for users or groups provisioned (registered) in Quick.
Choose tag-based rules only if you are using embedded dashboards and want to secure data for users not provisioned (unregistered users) in Quick.

claim: 1-click embedding suits an internal application where users must authenticate, giving a static embed code, while embedding with the Quick Sight APIs also suits an external application that anyone can access and gives a one-time code.
question: Which Quick embedding method works for an application anyone can access?

values.display: best for when you want to embed a Amazon Quick Sight dashboard in an internal application that users need to authenticate in to
an external application that anyone can access

evidence.quote: Using 1-click enterprise embedding is best for when you want to embed a Amazon Quick Sight dashboard in an internal application that users need to authenticate in to. When you copy the embed code, you get a static embed code that doesn't change.

Embedding with the Amazon Quick Sight API is best for when you want to embed the Amazon Quick Sight experience in an internal application that users must authenticate in to, or an external application that anyone can access. When you use the embedding API operations to generate an embed code, you get a one-time code.

claim: When Quick Sight queries data with Amazon Athena, Lake Formation adds its own grant and revoke permissions model on top of IAM, and you can use it instead of, or in addition to, scoped-down IAM policies.
question: How does Lake Formation secure data that Quick Sight queries through Athena?

values.display: Lake Formation adds to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions model
instead of, or in addition to, using scoped-down policies with IAM

evidence.quote: Lake Formation adds to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions model by providing its own permissions model that is applied to AWS analytics and machine learning services. This centrally defined permissions model controls data access at a granular level through a simple grant and revoke mechanism. You can use Lake Formation instead of, or in addition to, using scoped-down policies with IAM.
